title: Sadu Bedouin ground-loom weaving
summary: Bedouin weavers of Jordan stretch the warp flat along the ground, pegged at both ends, and weave sturdy goat-hair and wool strips for tents and saddlebags. Bands of diamonds, triangles and zigzags are built up row by row and always read the same from the left edge to the right.
howToPlay: Study the strip on the chart: each row is a band of wool in one colour and shape.
Choose a wool colour, then a pattern shape, and place it on the loom; its mirror partner on the other side appears at once.
Fill every band of the chart, then check your strip against it.
rules: Every strip is a mirror of itself: a shape placed on one side is also placed on the other.
Each cell takes one shape in one wool colour; placing the same again lifts it.
Your strip is judged cell by cell against the chart: shape and colour must both match.
Three charts are woven in turn: a tent strip, a saddlebag band and a wedding strip.
heritageNote: Sadu is a living craft of Bedouin women across Jordan and the Arabian Peninsula, where weaving on a ground loom has been handed from mother to daughter and is still practised in cooperatives today.
